title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Ventral cord syndrome, also known as anterior spinal cord syndrome, is a rare but time-sensitive myelopathy characterized by bilateral motor paralysis and loss of pain and temperature sensation, with preservation of vibration and proprioception. The condition most frequently arises from ischemia of the anterior spinal artery but may also result from traumatic, compressive, or perioperative aortic pathology, as well as profound hypotension. Pathophysiology involves selective injury to the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord, particularly affecting corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts while sparing the dorsal columns. Clinical differentiation from mimicking disorders such as transverse myelitis, demyelinating disease, or compressive lesions is crucial, as early recognition directly influences neurologic recovery. Magnetic resonance imaging with vascular assessment remains the cornerstone of diagnosis, supplemented by laboratory evaluation and hemodynamic monitoring. Prognosis depends on the speed of intervention, with delayed recognition often leading to irreversible paralysis and functional dependence.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through this course, clinicians gain the knowledge and skills to recognize the hallmark presentation of ventral cord syndrome, interpret emergent neuroimaging findings, and apply evidence-based management strategies. The curriculum emphasizes hemodynamic optimization, judicious use of decompressive surgery, and avoidance of ineffective or harmful interventions. Participants learn structured diagnostic algorithms, perioperative management principles, and rehabilitation and long-term follow-up strategies. Collaboration within an interprofessional team—including neurologists, neurosurgeons, intensivists, radiologists, rehabilitation specialists, and nurses—enhances diagnostic precision, reduces delays to definitive care, and promotes seamless transitions from acute stabilization to rehabilitation. Through coordinated workflows and shared decision-making, clinicians improve neurological recovery, minimize complications, and optimize quality of life for patients with ventral cord syndrome.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Objectives: Assess the onset, progression, and distribution of motor, sensory, and autonomic findings to accurately define the extent of anterior spinal cord involvement. Compare characteristic clinical features, MRI patterns, and vascular territories distinguishing ventral cord syndrome from transverse myelitis, demyelinating disease, and compressive lesions. Create comprehensive diagnostic pathways integrating MRI with vascular sequences, spinal angiography, and laboratory studies to expedite etiology determination. Apply effective strategies to enhance care coordination among interprofessional team members, facilitating positive outcomes for patients with ventral cord syndrome. title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Introduction
content: Ventral cord syndrome (VCS), also referred to as anterior cord syndrome or anterior spinal artery syndrome, is caused by any condition that leads to infarction of the ventral two-thirds of the spinal cord. Estimates for the incidence and prevalence of ventral cord syndrome vary, yet it is the most common type of spinal cord infarction. Patients with ventral cord syndrome present with impairments of both pain and temperature sensation while maintaining vibration and proprioception sensation. Motor deficits are noticeable both at and below the level of injury. Magnetic resonance imaging can visually assess the degree of spinal cord ischemia. Current treatment for ventral cord syndrome is primarily supportive and follows guidelines for cerebral ischemia, atherosclerotic vascular disease, and acute traumatic spinal cord injury.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Etiology
content: Ventral cord syndrome results from direct or indirect damage to the ventral spinal cord. A direct injury arises when the spinal cord is mechanically crushed or compressed, as in the case of an enlarging hematoma. Indirect injuries constitute the primary etiology of ventral cord syndrome, and the resultant tissue damage is secondary to the ischemia. The integrity of the aorta is critical for the proper perfusion of the ventral aspect of the spinal cord, and knowledge of vascular anatomy is required to understand this concept. The aorta gives rise to the subclavian arteries, which in turn give rise to the vertebral arteries. The vertebral arteries give rise to the anterior spinal artery (ASA), which supplies the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. Therefore, any condition that compromises the aorta, such as aortic dissection, may cause indirect injuries to the ventral cord. Ventral cord syndrome can also result from iatrogenic damage to the aorta following surgical complications during attempted vascular repairs or with prolonged clamping of the aorta. Other less common causes of infarcts to the ventral cord are intrinsic arterial occlusion due to emboli or atheroma of the ASA or the radicular branches. [1]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Etiology
content: The anterior aspect of the spinal cord is particularly susceptible to ischemia because the supplying vessels are end-arteries and typically have no anastomoses. ASA infarction may also occur due to impairment of perfusion via the great anterior radicular artery of Adamkiewicz, which is the major contributor to the caudal two-thirds of ASA in the lower thoracic and upper lumbar region (T5 to L2) of the spinal cord. Other causes of blood flow disruption in ASA include aneurysms, trauma, or syphilitic arteries. [2] Finally, hypotensive states, venous infarctions, multiple sclerosis, and cord impingement by fracture fragments are less common causes of vascular damage to the anterior cord.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Epidemiology
content: Currently, there are few epidemiological studies on nontraumatic spinal cord injury, and these do not allow for an accurate estimate of the actual incidence and prevalence. [3] As mentioned earlier, the leading cause of ventral cord syndrome is a non-traumatic ischemic injury. Acute spinal cord infarction is a rare disorder that accounts for only 8% of all myelopathies and not more than 1% of all strokes. [4] Ventral cord syndrome is the most common of all ischemic spinal cord syndromes. Many of the case series in the literature on ischemic lesions have relatively small cohorts; they demonstrate that the age range typically affected spans from the first to the tenth decade of life, with a median age in the sixth to seventh decade. [5]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pathophysiology
content: The anterior two-thirds of the cord contains significant tracts for the proper functioning of the central nervous system (CNS); injury impairs the actions of these tracts. Motor function impairment arises from damage to the efferent corticospinal tract, and sensory deficits occur from damage to the afferent spinothalamic and spinocerebellar tracts. Other symptoms of the syndrome will depend on where the cord was injured. In general, there is a risk for autonomic dysreflexia, sexual impairments, movement impediments, neuropathic pain, and neurogenic bladder and bowel. [6] The clinical onset of ventral cord syndrome is abrupt, with pain, flaccid paraplegia or tetraplegia below the lesion, and alterations in temperature and pain sensation. [7] Vibration, fine touch, and proprioception sensory modalities will not be affected, as these are relayed by the dorsal columns located in the posterior one-third of the cord and supplied by the 2 posterior spinal arteries.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: Ischemic and reperfusion injuries cause damage to the spinal cord by activating microglia and astrocytes, disrupting the blood-spinal cord barrier (BSCB), causing tissue edema, and inducing neutrophil influx. [8] A complex signaling cascade is triggered upon disruption of blood flow to the CNS, leading to neuronal destruction. Blood flow reduction and oxygen deprivation lead to ionic pump failure and anoxic depolarization, producing excess glutamate and intracellular calcium. Overactivation of the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) and α-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors, dysregulation of metabolic and mitochondrial activity, and loss of osmotic balance ultimately lead to excitotoxic cell death. This rise in calcium triggers the production of free radicals, cytotoxic edema, and increased nitric oxide generation, all of which contribute to cellular damage and loss. During the subacute stage, additional neuronal death is believed to result from the accompanying inflammatory response, oxidative stress, and activation of apoptosis pathways, which are also termed ‘reperfusion injury.’ [9]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Histopathology
content: On the other hand, mechanical trauma to the spinal cord results in injury during two separate phases. The initial direct trauma causes acute compression and disruption of axons and vasculature. In the second phase, a cascade of events in histology gets triggered as a result of the injury, including hemorrhage, edema, inflammation, demyelination, pathologic changes in the neurons and oligodendroglia, as well as microglial and astrocyte activation in an early stage. A later stage consists of scar formation, Wallerian degeneration, development of cysts and syrinx, and schwannosis. [8]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- History and Physical
content: A complete history is vital in determining the etiology of ventral cord syndrome. Neurological examination reveals complete motor deficiency, accompanied by loss of pain, temperature, and crude-touch sensations. Bilateral motor deficits will be relevant directly below the level of the lesion. In contrast, bilateral sensory deficits typically begin two to three dermatomal segments below the level of the lesion, as the spinothalamic tract ascends at least 2 to 3 segments before decussating at the anterior commissure. Early motor deficits due to spinal shock include flaccidity with absent reflexes, followed by a gradual return of the reflexes and increased tone or spasticity. Patients with ventral cord syndrome typically retain light touch, proprioception, and vibration sensations. Damage to the autonomic centers of the spine results in orthostatic hypotension, bladder and bowel incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. Also, patients often report a radicular or diffuse type of pain. [10]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Magnetic resonance (MR) imaging is the modality of choice for visually evaluating spinal cord ischemia, including axial and sagittal diffusion-weighted MR imaging examinations. Characteristic MR imaging features of acute spinal cord ischemia include diffusion restriction in the ASA territory on diffusion-weighted images and a pencil-like hyperintense signal on sagittal T2-weighted images, accompanied by cord enlargement, if present. Axial MR images show a central T2-hyperintense signal on either side of the median fissure because there is relative sparing of the peripheral and posterior cords due to collateral vessels from the vascular pial plexus and posterior spinal arteries. Sometimes, a central T2-hyperintense signal resembling "snake eyes" appears in the anterior spinal cord on either side of the median fissure. Although this finding is considered specific for spinal cord infarction, it can also occur in association with compression myelopathy and various infectious or inflammatory spinal conditions. [10] MR angiography or CT angiography are appropriate adjunctive modalities for further delineation of vascular pathology.  Digital subtraction angiography will delineate the vascular anatomy, which is necessary in cases that require an interventional procedure. [11]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Evaluation
content: Laboratory workup consists of a complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, electrolyte levels, glucose, creatinine, cholesterol levels, liver function tests, protein electrophoresis, coagulation tests, and an electrocardiogram. These tests screen for conditions that cause ischemic damage to vessels, such as diabetes mellitus, atherosclerosis, and hypercholesterolemia. Serological tests for borreliosis, Lyme disease, syphilis, human immunodeficiency virus, human T-cell lymphotropic virus, and herpes virus are necessary if infections cause the infarct. Patients can also undergo screening for antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, which may indicate vasculitis as a potential cause. The cerebrospinal fluid should undergo analysis for cell count, glucose and protein levels, and oligoclonal bands, as well as for the presence of antibodies to particular pathogens. CSF analysis will likely show increased protein concentration without pleocytosis or intrathecal synthesis of immunoglobulins. [12]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Current treatment is mainly supportive and follows guidelines for cerebral ischemia, atherosclerotic vascular disease, and acute traumatic spinal cord injury. The primary focus is to address the underlying cause, which includes managing fever and glycemic control and anticoagulation, antiplatelet, and thromboprophylaxis therapy. [9] . Protecting airways and maintaining blood pressure support in an acute setting is paramount. If the patient is hypotensive, then blood pressure must be raised by using phenylephrine, norepinephrine, and high-dose dopamine. For blood pressure reduction, preferred medications include labetalol, esmolol, and nicardipine. [13] Risk factors associated with more severe spinal cord strokes include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, and elevated blood glucose on admission (regardless of whether the patient has diabetes mellitus). Cardiovascular risk factors are well-established etiologies of cerebral stroke. Treatment and prevention of these risk factors should be essential in acute spinal cord stroke management. [14]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: In most cases, management is primarily limited to improving symptoms and preventing future complications. The patient needs to receive education on how to adapt to their new body and condition. Impairments during hospitalization and after discharge must be addressed, including limitations in mobility and activities of daily living, bladder, bowel, and sexual dysfunction. Pressure ulcers, pain, and spasticity are common complications that require appropriate management. After discharge, patients must obtain and be able to safely use the necessary adaptive equipment to optimize their functional independence. A particular focus must be given to the patient's psychosocial function and participation to achieve increased independence, quality of life, and a better prognosis.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Treatment / Management
content: Studies have shown the benefit of lumbar CSF drainage and the elevation of mean arterial pressure from 60 to 90 or 100 mm Hg in avoiding ischemic injury during vascular repair surgery.  Surgical maneuvers such as aortic cross-clamping and retraction can produce acute elevations in CSF pressure, which hinders venous outflow, leading to ischemia. Hence, this ischemia may be reversible in some cases by utilizing CSF drainage while supporting systemic blood pressure. [15] [16] Steroids can also be added to this regimen to reduce cytotoxicity and vasogenic edema. Left heart bypass maintains perfusion to the distal aorta and iliac arteries for open procedures. [9]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Differential Diagnosis
content: Ischemic spinal cord injury is a rare and often misdiagnosed disease. Multiple sclerosis can show similar MRI findings to spinal cord infarctions, thus risking confusion. Spinal cord neoplasms should be in the differential diagnosis (see Image. Spinal Cord Syndromes). However, tumors typically have a slow clinical onset, unlike the acute presentation of spinal cord ischemia. Transverse myelitis is another condition with a similar clinical presentation to infarctions, yet the onset is not quite as acute. Venous congestive myelopathy should also be on the differential. Yet, it differs from infarcts in that it will present with prominent enlarged pial veins with the involvement of the cord's central and peripheral white matter. [17]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Current preclinical research is studying promising pharmacological agents as a possible treatment for ischemic spinal cord injuries (SCI). Neuroprotective therapies are based on limiting secondary injury after the initial damage by modulating inflammation, reducing cell death, and protecting against excitotoxicity. Currently, no proven pharmacological therapies for human spinal cord injury provide neuroprotection. Studies have used propofol, thymoquinone, minocycline, erythropoietin, and curcumin as potential neuroprotective pharmacological agents. Antioxidants protect against the oxidative damage caused by secondary neurodegeneration after acute SCI. Antioxidants stabilize mitochondrial bioenergetics, protect neurons, and achieve modest neurological recovery after injury.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pertinent Studies and Ongoing Trials
content: Emerging research is focusing on measures that could help prevent ischemic spinal cord injury during vascular surgery. Hypothermia preserves tissue integrity during periods of interrupted blood flow; animal studies suggest that hypothermia suppresses excitatory synaptic transmission and reduces neuronal injury. Hyperbaric oxygen increases tissue oxygenation and metabolism in penumbral tissue. Ischemic preconditioning is a way to prepare tissue for the ischemic state, thus rendering it more resistant to a hypoxic insult. Numerous preclinical investigations have examined the molecular pathways and potential benefits of pre- and postischemic preconditioning, yielding encouraging results. Other studies examine how to counteract apoptosis, which leads to neuronal cell death. Many of the current treatments for spinal cord infarcts show only modest improvements in the functional outcome if used as monotherapy, which is probably attributable to the fact that many factors lead to the development of permanent neurological deficits. Thus, future treatment trials should consider a combined and multimodal treatment approach. [9]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Staging
content: Acute spinal cord injury occurs in 2 phases. The initial injury phase results from the initial insult to the cord, whether caused by direct mechanical damage or disruption of blood vessels, axons, or cell membranes. This initial insult triggers a pathophysiological cascade within seconds—the secondary injury phase results from ongoing endogenous triggers that cause tissue destruction. The secondary phase can be further subdivided into the immediate (less than 2 hours), early acute (less than 48 hours), and subacute (less than 2 weeks) phases. [18]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Prognosis
content: Individuals with spinal cord infarction have a better prognosis than those with cerebral stroke. A study of 30 patients with spinal cord injury looked at the long-term prognosis by following them for a mean of 7.1 years. The study's results concluded that long-term mortality was lower in patients with spinal cord infarcts after adjusting for age and functional scores in the acute phase. The better prognosis is likely because spinal cord infarction patients have lower frequencies of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and cardiac disease. [19] The same study found that many patients with spinal cord infarction made significant clinical improvements, which improved prognosis. The determination was that in the long run, most of the surviving patients over 60 years of age at the time of injury had returned to their jobs. On the other hand, re-employment was lower among stroke patients less than 60 years at the onset, even when their functional scores are better than those of spinal cord infarction patients. Cerebral infarction patients are likely to have cognitive deficits. Yet, the prevalence of cognitive deficits is rare among spinal cord infarction patients and probably does not differ from that in other hospitalized patients with an equally serious condition. [14] [19] Chronic pain is a common finding in spinal cord infarction patients, with up to 79% of patients reporting chronic pain on follow-up. There is also a low incidence of depression in these patients, which is likely attributable to their preserved cognitive functioning. Higher mortality in the spinal cord infarction population is associated with older age, the severity of impairments in the acute phase, and the presence of peripheral vascular disease. [14] The prognosis for ventral cord syndrome will depend in large part on the initial degree of impairment upon injury. Studies conclude that the less severe the impairment, the better the outcome. [20] [21] Further, the initial severity of the impairment, particularly motor deficits, is the most reliable predictor of functional recovery.
contents: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Prognosis. Individuals with spinal cord infarction have a better prognosis than those with cerebral stroke. A study of 30 patients with spinal cord injury looked at the long-term prognosis by following them for a mean of 7.1 years. The study's results concluded that long-term mortality was lower in patients with spinal cord infarcts after adjusting for age and functional scores in the acute phase. The better prognosis is likely because spinal cord infarction patients have lower frequencies of atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and cardiac disease. [19] The same study found that many patients with spinal cord infarction made significant clinical improvements, which improved prognosis. The determination was that in the long run, most of the surviving patients over 60 years of age at the time of injury had returned to their jobs. On the other hand, re-employment was lower among stroke patients less than 60 years at the onset, even when their functional scores are better than those of spinal cord infarction patients. Cerebral infarction patients are likely to have cognitive deficits. Yet, the prevalence of cognitive deficits is rare among spinal cord infarction patients and probably does not differ from that in other hospitalized patients with an equally serious condition. [14] [19] Chronic pain is a common finding in spinal cord infarction patients, with up to 79% of patients reporting chronic pain on follow-up. There is also a low incidence of depression in these patients, which is likely attributable to their preserved cognitive functioning. Higher mortality in the spinal cord infarction population is associated with older age, the severity of impairments in the acute phase, and the presence of peripheral vascular disease. [14] The prognosis for ventral cord syndrome will depend in large part on the initial degree of impairment upon injury. Studies conclude that the less severe the impairment, the better the outcome. [20] [21] Further, the initial severity of the impairment, particularly motor deficits, is the most reliable predictor of functional recovery.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Complications
content: Ventral cord syndrome (VCS) shares similar complications to other spinal cord injuries and diseases. With that said, spinal cord injury increases the risk of many medical complications and morbidities, most of which result from the paralysis and extreme inactivity. Physical inactivity itself is a contributing factor to insulin resistance, carbohydrate metabolism disorders, and dyslipidemia. Calcifications in the coronary arteries are more prevalent in spinal cord injury patients as compared to their able-bodied counterparts. Patients are at increased risk for fractures and osteoporosis because of immobility. There is a reduction in circulating growth hormone and testosterone. The lifetime risk of pressure ulcers is estimated to be around 50% in patients with spinal cord injury. There are also adverse changes to soft tissue body composition with increased adiposity and reduced skeletal muscle. Diffuse gastrointestinal tract dysmotility often brings about other problems, such as gastrointestinal reflux and difficulty evacuating. Respiratory dysfunction can arise depending on the level and completeness of the injury. Patients with spinal cord injury above the sixth thoracic vertebra have deficits in both cardiac and peripheral vascular mechanisms, which are needed to maintain blood pressure; thus, they are often hypotensive. Persistent and orthostatic hypotension can predispose to cognitive impairments. [22]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Since postoperative treatments for ventral cord syndrome are often ineffective, measures to prevent perioperative cord ischemia should include avoiding anemia, systemic hypotension, and hyperextension/hyperflexion during positioning. Efforts must be made to minimize any surgical accidents resulting in vascular dissection. [23] During procedures involving interventions on the thoracoabdominal aorta, early detection of spinal cord ischemia can be achieved through neuromonitoring with evoked potentials in the anesthetized patient and with a neurologic examination in the awake patient. [24]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Postoperative and Rehabilitation Care
content: Tetraplegia and paraplegia are among the most devastating consequences of VCS. These movement impediments significantly impact the individual's and society's medical, social, and financial costs. Since no current treatment can reverse VCS, patients must receive rehabilitation focused on improving independence and quality of life, all while preventing secondary complications of spinal cord injury. Patients are candidates for various forms of rehabilitation, including, but not limited to, physical therapy, occupational therapy, vocational therapy, and neuropsychological therapy.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: During hospitalization, patients require instruction on adapting to life after VCS. Follow-up visits also provide an opportunity for support and patient education. The journey of adjustment to disability is an evolving, dynamic, general process from which the patient progresses to an optimal state of person-environment congruence. The clinical team should focus on instructing and coaching the patient through this process. [25]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Patients must receive training in developing effective coping strategies; literature supports the role of these strategies during the psychological adjustment phase. Results from a study by Kennedy et al showed that 45 patients who participated in a coping training program showed lower scores for depression and anxiety compared to a control group that received the standard of care. [26] Psychological resources refer to a person's inner, health-protecting, and health-promoting capacities, representing a source or means to cope with challenging situations. They may include abilities, skills, knowledge, experience, talents, strengths, and behavioral patterns of a person. Clinicians must help patients strengthen their psychological resources to support a successful adjustment. [25]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: The patient must receive counseling on the importance of participating in sports and exercising to improve their health. The literature consistently shows that exercise improves functional performance, psychological well-being, and social integration. Before engaging in physical activity, an appropriate screening must be performed to determine the proper exercise prescription, identify any necessary precautions, and provide modifications required for the physical activity. Education also centers on other social aspects of a patient's life. Clinicians play a crucial role in helping individuals engage in gainful employment. The medical team needs to assess and provide options and modifications for transportation. Transportation is vital to independence and social integration in the spinal cord injury community.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Deterrence and Patient Education
content: Hospital discharge offers clinicians an excellent opportunity to educate patients, their families, friends, and caregivers. The medical team must assess the options and equipment available that facilitate the patient's life and integration into society. Discharge planning should consider preparing for emergencies and complications, establishing follow-up appointments and support, providing the patient with appropriate medical equipment, and conducting a home assessment.

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Clinical Pearls:
content: "Owl's Eyes" Sign on MRI : Axial T2-weighted MRI often shows bilateral hyperintensities in the anterior horns, resembling "owl's eyes." This finding is particular to spinal cord infarction but appears in only 4% to 35% of cases. An initial normal MRI does not exclude VCS; repeat imaging within 24–48 hours is critical if clinical suspicion remains. [27] [28] [29]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Clinical Pearls:
content: Dissociated Sensory Loss : The classic triad—motor paralysis, loss of pain/temperature sensation, and preserved proprioception—localizes damage to the territory of the anterior spinal artery. This pattern arises from disrupting the spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, sparing the dorsal columns. [10]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Clinical Pearls:
content: Autonomic Crises : Lesions above T6 may cause neurogenic shock (hypotension, bradycardia) acutely and autonomic dysreflexia chronically. The latter is a hypertensive emergency triggered by visceral stimuli (eg, bladder distension), requiring immediate intervention to prevent intracranial hemorrhage or pulmonary edema. [10]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Disposition and Management:
content: Acute Phase: Intensive care unit (ICU) admission is mandatory for high cervical injuries (C1–C5) due to the risk of respiratory failure from phrenic nerve involvement. Neurogenic shock often requires hemodynamic support with vasopressors (eg, norepinephrine). [31] Surgical decompression within 24 hours is indicated for compressive etiologies (eg, epidural hematoma, traumatic fractures), reducing ICU stays and complications. [32] Rehabilitation: Early mobilization with  weight-supported treadmill training improves ambulation potential. Multidisciplinary care (physical/occupational therapy, bladder retraining, psychological support) mitigates long-term disability. [32]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Common Pitfalls:
content: Misdiagnosis : VCS mimics transverse myelitis, multiple sclerosis, or compressive myelopathies. Pitfall : Delaying MRI or attributing symptoms to psychogenic causes. Solution : Emergent MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging and angiography to assess vascular integrity. [33] Steroid Misuse : High-dose steroids (eg, methylprednisolone) lack evidence for ischemic VCS and may exacerbate hyperglycemia or infection. Reserve for traumatic edema or concurrent inflammatory conditions. [34] Overlooking Aortic Pathology : Up to 30% of cases link to aortic dissection or surgery. Pitfall : Focusing solely on spinal imaging without evaluating the aorta. Solution : CT angiography or transesophageal echocardiography for high-risk patients. [35] Autonomic Overlook: Failure to monitor for autonomic dysreflexia in hospitalized patients. Pitfall : Uncontrolled hypertension misinterpreted as essential HTN. Solution : Immediate bladder/bowel decompression and nitrates for BP control. [36]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Pearls and Other Issues -- Prognosis and Innovations:
content: VCS has the poorest functional outcomes among spinal cord syndromes, with mortality rates of 9% to 23%. Emerging therapies, such as epidural stimulation and stem cell transplantation, show promise in preclinical studies but remain investigational. [37]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Patient participation is a core component of high-quality healthcare and is associated with improvement of self-care, functioning, and satisfaction. A literature review considers patients as experts on their bodies, symptoms, and situations. As experts, patients’ experiential knowledge is now considered complementary to medical professionals’ knowledge and essential for successful treatment and improving the quality of care. [38]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Participation becomes particularly crucial during spinal cord injury rehabilitation, where the health care staff comprises a broad range of professionals, including nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, social workers, and physicians. Patients must be encouraged to engage in the management plan as a team member. A level V evidence study conducted in Sweden found that information tailored to the individual and delivered promptly is essential for enabling patients to actively and meaningfully participate in decisions regarding their care and rehabilitation. [39]

content: Recovery from spinal cord injury relies on the care received at each point along this recovery timeline. A systematic review analyzed the treatment literature on spinal cord injury to facilitate the practice of evidence-based medicine and best clinical practice. Fehlings and coworkers summarized the most notable findings in the research and offered evidence-based care recommendations. Some of their most essential proposals are as follows: Patients should be placed on a cervical collar, head immobilizers, and a spinal board before being transported to a hospital. Outcomes show more improvement by management in specialized centers with access to intensive care. [40]

title: Ventral Cord Syndrome -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Treatment of acute spinal cord injury is an interprofessional effort that begins shortly after the injury, continues during the acute care setting, and, in some cases, continues for the remainder of the patient's life. An interprofessional team approach that includes physicians, specialists, therapists, and specialty-trained nurses will lead to optimal care and the most satisfactory clinical outcomes.
